result:
Solution 3 is the only one consistent with the cases I could verify by hand.

**Reduction.** Erasing with $k=0$ wipes the whole board, so it always loses. A move with $k\ge1$ removes one dyadic class $\{s : s\equiv n \pmod{2^k}\}$ intersected with the board. Since any single element can be isolated with large $k$, a player can always remove exactly one number.

**Small cases (P = Geoff loses, N = Geoff wins):**
- A single number is P.
- Any 2- or 3-element board is N, since some class splits off exactly one element.
- A 4-element board is P exactly when its first parity-type split is 2–2.
- Any 5-element board is N.
- $\{1,\dots,4\}$ is P (split 2–2).
- $\{1,\dots,6\}$ is P: its parity classes have size 3 (both N), and every 2-element class removal leaves a 4-set with a 1–3 split.
- $\{1,\dots,7\}$ is N: removing the evens leaves $\{1,3,5,7\}$, which is P.
- $\{1,\dots,8\}$ is N: removing the odds leaves $\{2,4,6,8\}$, which is P.
- $\{1,\dots,9\}$ is N: removing the odds leaves $\{2,4,6,8\}$, which is P.
- $\{1,\dots,10\}$ is P: I checked every legal move (all 9-element residuals, all 8-element residuals, and the class removals) and each leads to an N-position.
- $\{1,\dots,12\}$ is N: removing the odds leaves $\{2,4,\dots,12\}$, which is P.

**Comparison with the three answers:**
- Solution 1 says 10 is N, but 10 is P. Its answer is wrong.
- Solution 2 says 8 is P, but 8 is N. Its answer is wrong.
- Solution 3 predicts P exactly for $N\in\{1\}\cup\{4^m\}\cup\{N\equiv 2 \pmod 4,\ N\ge 6\}$. This matches every case above: P at 1, 4, 6, 10 and N at 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 12.

I have not verified the pattern beyond $N=12$, so this relies on the pattern holding in general. The smallest 20 winning values from Solution 3 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 15, 17, 19, 20, 21, 23, 24, 25, 27, 28, 29. Their sum is 318, which I confirmed.

CHOICE: 3
